_meta: DRAFT, AWAITING OPERATOR REVIEW. Every claim below is transcribed from the PhyTS benchmark paper or measured from the released data; nothing is invented. Provenance per block: `interpret` line 1 from PhyTS appendix D.2 (R-squared is computed against the evaluation set's own variance) and line 3 from PhyTS section 3.2 (the near-core rotation rates follow an asymptotic approximation calibrated on a restricted stellar regime, so reference frequencies are approximate outside it); `interpret` line 2 measured from the released manifest, not stated in the paper. `propose` lines 1-2 from PhyTS Table 2 and Table 10 (Stars & Exoplanets regression R-squared column); line 3 from PhyTS section 3.2 (g-mode pulsators, rotation shifts pulsation frequencies); line 4 from PhyTS appendix D.4, which attributes the causal decoders' weakness on zero-shot regression to a last-token representation optimised for next-step prediction rather than for summarising global properties. `implement` from this task package's own declared forward contract and preprocessing authority. `tune` from the experiment's own frozen budgets. This artifact is the PRIOR arm's treatment; the no-prior arm receives no advice file at all.
interpret: The selection metric R-squared is normalized by the EVALUATION SET'S OWN total sum of squares. Two R-squared values are therefore comparable only when computed over the same evaluation population: a value from a reduced-portion round is not comparable to a full-validation value, and neither is comparable to a published test-set figure. When you need an error that does not move with the evaluation population, read the secondary RMSE, which carries physical units of cycles per day.

The target is derived per LIGHT CURVE rather than per star, so the same star observed in different sectors can carry different target values. Measured on the released data, a model that predicted each star's mean target perfectly would score R-squared 0.9163 on train and 0.9763 on validation. That is a label-noise ceiling, not a goal; published baselines sit far below it, so it is not currently what limits performance.

The published reference frequencies follow an asymptotic approximation calibrated on a restricted stellar regime, so they are approximate outside that regime. Treat a residual pattern concentrated in a few curves as possible label uncertainty rather than automatically as a model deficiency, and say which of the two an observation supports.
analysis: Characterize only the authorized training and validation inputs. Measured properties of the inputs are findings; statements about the held-out population are not available and must not be inferred.

The released light curves come from two different observing cadences, 30-minute and 10-minute, so a fixed-length window covers a different physical duration depending on which mission observed a star. Quantifying how that mixture is distributed across the training population is a useful measured finding.
Report the target distribution as measured, including its extremes. An unresolved question about the data is not a finding.
propose: Structured state-space models outperform convolutional and zero-shot foundation-model approaches on this exact task in the published benchmark: S4D reaches R-squared 0.665, CNN 0.617 and LinOSS 0.612, against a mean-predictor baseline of -0.017. Prefer an architecture that integrates information across the full sequence over one that only aggregates local features.

Capacity is NOT the lever here. Across the published sweep, all three supervised baselines peak near 300 thousand parameters, and the best of them DROPS from 0.665 to 0.522 when scaled to roughly 700 thousand. Start near the published scale rather than assuming that a larger model is a better one, and justify a substantially larger candidate with measured evidence rather than with capacity alone.

The physical signal is periodic. Rotation shifts the frequencies of the star's gravity-mode pulsations, so the information lives in the frequency content of the variability rather than in its amplitude or in where a feature falls inside the window. An architecture or a pooling choice that is translation-sensitive is working against the physics.

The quantity being predicted is a GLOBAL property of the whole sequence. In the published evaluation, representations that summarise the entire window outperform last-token representations optimised for next-step prediction, which were systematically weakest on this regression. Prefer a head that reads a whole-sequence summary.
implement: The output head must be exactly [B, 1] with NO squashing activation. The target is an unbounded real quantity that includes a small number of negative values, so a ReLU or sigmoid output would make part of the target range unreachable and would cap the achievable score for a reason unrelated to the science.

Padding is part of the input distribution, not an edge case. Most Primary-Mission curves are shorter than the fixed window and are right-padded with their last observed value after normalization, so a large fraction of every batch ends in a constant tail. A model that cannot tolerate that tail will fail on the majority of the training population rather than on a rare case.
tune: The budget is 8 GiB of VRAM with 5 minutes for a trial round and 15 minutes for a formal round. At the published parameter scale a candidate trains well inside that envelope, so prefer testing more distinct hypotheses over extending any single run.

The training objective is yours to choose; it is deliberately not declared by the task. The selection metric is R-squared and is unaffected by that choice, so state what each attempt was testing rather than tuning the loss toward the metric.
